{"number":1494,"title":"The executor carries repo variables as one `toJSON(vars)` bag","body":"A task needing a repository **variable** paid what a task needing a secret pays: the executor workflow had to name it, `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot write, so a new value meant a human-merged PR in every member — the coupling that wedged one in #1296. One static line ends it for variables: ```yaml CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }} ``` ## Why the `toJSON(secrets)` reasoning does not carry `toJSON(secrets)` is the shape GitHub's [malicious-workflow detection](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-github-actions-holds-potentially-malicious-workflows-for-approval/) flags (#1336) — every run parks with zero jobs until a person clicks Approve, silently and fleet-wide. `vars` is not that shape: - The safeguard's stated threat model is credential theft. GitHub's own docs define `vars` as the non-sensitive context — *"Variables provide a way to store and reuse non-sensitive configuration information […] By default, variables render unmasked in your build outputs. If you need greater security for sensitive information, such as passwords, use secrets instead."* Serialising it exfiltrates nothing the build logs do not already show. - `${{ toJSON(vars) }}` is a mainstream pattern with Marketplace actions built to consume it; flagging it would be a mass false-positive event. - **We already field it.** `packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml:62` and `static-site-deploy-pages.yml:70` have both passed `toJSON(vars)` since before the safeguard shipped, without one park. GitHub publishes no detection signals, thresholds or false-positive rate, so this is inference plus our own field evidence rather than a guarantee. `vars-bag.mjs` carries that caveat and the symptom to watch for — #1336's `action_required` with zero jobs, which reads exactly like an idle queue — at the site rather than only here. ## What the reader does differently from the secrets bag Two points, each stated where it is made: - **No per-task selection.** `required_secrets` narrows a task's blast radius; `vars` is non-sensitive by construction, so there is nothing to narrow and a declaration would buy only a second place to keep in sync. - **Additive, never overwriting.** The secrets bag replaced named lines and is subtracted from the inherited environment first, so it has nothing to collide with. This one lands on a live runner environment it does not own, and a repo variable is any name an owner typed into a settings box — a repo with a variable called `PATH` or `HOME` must not reach into a task subprocess and replace the runner's own. The JSON parse both bags share moves to `env-bag.mjs` rather than being copied. ## Folders touched 
packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/   env-bag.mjs (new) holds the parse both bags share; vars-bag.mjs
                                (new) reads CLAUDINITE_VARS additively; secrets-bag.mjs now
                                delegates its parse; code-work-run.mjs's taskEnv unpacks the vars
                                bag and strips both raw blobs before handing the env on.

.github/workflows/              The canon's own executor gains the static CLAUDINITE_VARS line,
                                edited in the same commit as the stub beside it.

packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/   The executor stub gains the same line. The scheduler stub is
                                untouched — it runs no task code.

vendoring/rehearsal/            A vars-bag-executor fixture: the far side of this PR converging
                                green.
## Assurance Each of the three assurances was written first and seen to fail before the code existed: the reader's tests, the stub-shape assertions, and the `taskEnv` test. The `toJSON(secrets)` guard stays exactly as strict, and gains a sibling pinning the vars line **present** in the executor stub and **absent** from the scheduler run. `consumer-safe-change` asked for a migration record or a rehearsal fixture — the change is genuinely additive, so the fixture is the honest answer, per that check's own fix text. `stamping-executor` already covers the near side every member sits on until its own workflow lands, where the bag is absent and `varsEnv` contributes nothing. Full suite green (2813 pass, 0 fail); `check_the_work` and `check_the_world` both 0 blocking. ## One thing left for you The line reaches existing members only through a per-member PR, since this is a stub change and `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot write. That is a one-time cost paid to end the recurring one. Whether to drive it now through Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` is a fleet-wide action and yours to call — I have not dispatched anything. Closes #1492 Refs #1336 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_012NwPTckVyUFwb6dMSuoH9s --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_012NwPTckVyUFwb6dMSuoH9s)_","state":"closed","draft":false,"merged":true,"mergeable_state":"unknown","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1494","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"merged_by":"missingbulb","head":{"ref":"claude/github-secrets-env-vars-xms47c","sha":"a477cee995cfeeb46312b7d8a56d24e9ece375fd","repo":{"full_name":"missingbulb/Claudinite"}},"base":{"ref":"main","sha":"823eb5b6f073572dda4b54af5cdda364e608063d","repo":{"full_name":"missingbulb/Claudinite"}},"additions":206,"deletions":18,"changed_files":12,"commits":1,"created_at":"2026-08-31T09:29:05Z","updated_at":"2026-08-31T09:45:09Z","closed_at":"2026-08-31T09:45:07Z","merged_at":"2026-08-31T09:45:07Z"}

{"number":1534,"title":"Coded production validations: URL probes judged as code-work","body":"Closes #1530

A verification whose artifact is a live URL — a Pages site, a deployed config — could not run at all: the queue's only runner was an agentic session, which has no egress, and #1184/#1288 parked exactly that way. This adds the **coded form**: declarative probes a code worker fetches and judges Action-side, where egress exists.

Three commits, in dependency order:

1. **The requeue protocol** (`code-work.mjs`, `queue/code-work-run.mjs`, `queue/executor.mjs`). A worker printing `claudinite-requeue:  — ` before a clean exit has the executor stamp the item's `Not-before` (machine half), strike its claim, and return the item to blocked — the third answer an exit code could not give (0 closes done, non-zero parks). Honoured only on an OK exit; an unreadable instant parks loudly.
2. **The `verify-production` task** (`claudinite-tasks/tasks/verify-production/`): agentless, `frequency: manual`, routed to by `Task: claudinite-tasks/verify-production` on a marked issue. `probes.mjs` is the grammar's one home — `Live-probe:`/`Verify-probe:` lines, each ` :: ` (`status`, `[not ]contains`, `[not ]matches`, and `json` path ops including a segment-wise-numeric `>=` for dotted version stamps). Both classes required: liveness failing → requeue by `Retry-every:`; a verify probe failing while live → reopen `Original-issue:` with what was asserted and what was read; all passing → close with the evidence.

{"number":1493,"title":"converge-item.mjs is the session's transition, and says so","body":"Closes #1491

Started stacked on #1490; that merged mid-flight, so this is rebased onto `main` and the diff is this change alone.

## The scope question, answered from the code

`queue/instructions.md` step 6 is this file's **only** caller. No `.github/workflows/*.yml` names it; no module imports `convergeItem`, `convergeOps`, `sessionScript` or `canReachRepo` outside the pack's own tests; the Actions side converges through `executor.mjs`'s own `converge(...)`. It is session-only — so the two scopes were already two files, and this one was just carrying a REST path duplicating the other. No split needed; the header now says which scope this is.

## Why the dead path was not merely dead

`main()` probed for REST first and treated its absence as the fallback. The one environment that runs this script is the one with no REST route, so a session met a `console.error` and a non-zero exit *before* it met the path written for it, then needed a second run behind `CLAUDINITE_ITEM_JSON`.

Sessions read that first result as breakage and stopped. The item kept `task:status:running-agent` until the janitor's 3h leash, and rule B parks a dead claim `needs-human-decision` unconditionally (`queue-sweep.mjs:95`) — so a run that did its work correctly became a human park.

Five items sampled across five repos and five tasks are all exactly this: [MissingBulbWebsite#240](https://github.com/missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite/issues/240), [ClaudiniteWebsite#308](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/308), [VascularColoring#159](https://github.com/missingbulb/VascularColoring/issues/159), [CrosswordChat#307](https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/issues/307), [Claudinite#1376](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1376). Three should have closed `done`; two are approvals holding a finished PR. None is a decision anyone owes an answer to.

And because a `decision` park does not block its lane, the standing slot frees, the task re-files on the next anchor, fails the same way and parks again — which is where the fleet's duplicate items and duplicate PRs come from. One defect, three symptoms.

## What changed

The header states the scope — one caller, no network, every line assuming MCP — and the code matches it. The file plans a transition and prints it addressed to the session's own tools. **Printing is the success**: stdout, exit 0, never a fallback. The item is handed in with `--item-file` rather than through a second run behind an environment variable; a file rather than an argument because an item's body is prose of arbitrary length and shell-quoting one is a bug waiting for the first apostrophe. `CLAUDINITE_ITEM_JSON` still reads, for a member whose `instructions.md` is a cycle behind.

`convergeOps` and `sessionScript` are unchanged in behaviour.

### By folder

```
packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/
  converge-item.mjs   header states the session-only, MCP-only scope; REST
                      executor (convergeItem, canReachRepo) and its
                      signals/gh.mjs and github.mjs imports removed; main() is
                      one path — item in via --item-file, script out on stdout,
                      exit 0
  instructions.md     step 6 rewritten to the two-call shape: read the item,
                      run the command, make the calls it prints
```

## Proof

Every behavioural change had its test written and watched fail first — 3 failing before, 13 passing after in `converge-session.test.mjs`.

`converge-item.test.mjs` keeps **all nineteen** assertions rather than losing them with the executor: they drive the same ops through a local applier, because what they pin — five side effects, in order, once, on the item held and nothing else — is the planner's contract and outlived its transport.

Full CI glob before the rebase: 2,391 pass, 0 fail. After the rebase, the pack's own 327 queue tests pass and `ci-work-scope --branch` reports 0 blocking over the 6 changed files — including the `pack-version-bumped` gate that #1482 caught being skipped. `claudinite-tasks` goes to `60831.2` with its `VERSIONS.md` row.

## What this does not fix

The 128 already-parked R5 items stay parked; this stops new ones being created. Draining the existing pile is separate work, and the mislabelled ones need re-reading before anyone treats them as questions someone owes an answer to.

{"number":1546,"title":"Never stamp a pack that still owes a withheld workflow file, and re-reach the five members it stranded","body":"Closes #1545

Five members are stamped past `claudinite-tasks` 60831.6 with no `CLAUDINITE_VARS` line in their live executor, and no converge can reach them. This fixes the cause and re-opens a route to the five.

## The defect

A migration record targeting `.github/workflows/` cannot be written by the converge — GitHub rejects the whole ref for a `GITHUB_TOKEN` push under that path — so the withhold lane stages it to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` and the apply stage delivers it on a credential that may write there.

The run stamped the owning pack regardless. That claims a delivery that has not happened, and it is unrecoverable rather than merely early:

1. `migrationApplies` is `want > have`, so the stamp immediately puts the record out of range — it stops applying and stops vendoring.
2. The next cycle's staging sweep reads the undelivered file as a leftover and deletes it.

Both copies of the content are then gone. Every signal stays green: the run succeeds, the stamp reads current, and `fleet-baseline` — which follows members to canon's stamped versions — reports success. A forced baseline did exactly that in 4m35s while five members were missing the delivery.

## The fix

**The stamp** skips a pack that finished the run owing a withheld file, scoped to that pack. The record stays applicable, so the next cycle stages the delivery again — a merged-but-undelivered PR becomes self-healing instead of a silent permanent loss. Attribution happens as each write occurs rather than by counting `withheld` afterwards, because that list is de-duplicated by path: two records from different packs naming one workflow path would otherwise stamp the pack whose content is the one actually staged.

**The worker's "nothing changed" guard** now lets an apply-stage terminal through. Holding the stamp removed the only thing that reliably dirtied the tree on a withholding cycle, so a re-staging cycle can leave `git status` clean — and the guard returns before the PR is opened, while the apply-stage request is written after it. Left unfixed, this fix would have reintroduced the same silent loss one step further along.

## Re-reaching the five

Nothing lowers a stamp already written, so the five need a record above where they landed. `2026-09-01-executor-vars-redelivery` carries the rewrite at 60901.1, and its `appliesTo` reads the destination's own content — inert on the eight that received the line normally, and safe on a member below 60831.6 where both records are in range.

The block is **copied rather than imported**. An import of the original resolves in the canon but not on a member: the vendor set carries only records that still apply, and the members this exists for are exactly the ones the original no longer applies to. The import dangles, the pack fails `pack-independence`, and `packUpdate` returns `needs-human` — the converge stops landing entirely, wedging all thirteen members instead of repairing five. The copy is pinned by a rewrite-equality assertion plus a new test refusing any record that imports another record.

Named `-redelivery` rather than `-bag-redeliver` because `migrationActive` matches a slug by substring: any name containing the original's slug would keep it reading as active forever.

## Verification

Lifecycle simulations driving the real flow against a member tree in the five's exact state (`claudinite-tasks` 60831.9, executor without the line):

| | cycle 1 | cycle 2 | cycle 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stranded, apply stage delivers** | withheld, stamp held 60831.9 | stamp 60901.1, line present | stable |
| **Stranded, apply stage fails again** | withheld, stamp held | re-staged, nothing lost | re-staged |
| **Healthy (the eight)** | inert, stamp 60901.1 | stable | — |

The middle row is the reported bug: that path previously deleted the staged file and put the record permanently out of range.

- Every new test seen failing first, on the real defect — the stamp (`60831.9` where `60831.5` is owed), the sibling import, the worker guard reverted to its old condition, and the attribution reverted to the count.
- Full suite: 2917 tests, 0 failures. `check_the_world`: 0 blocking, 87 advisory — identical to `main` with the branch stashed.

## Deliberately not in this PR

Both found by an adversarial review of this branch and filed rather than folded in:

- **#1555** — the staging sweep deletes on "I didn't write it this pass", which is not "it was delivered". The stamp hold narrows that window without making the criterion correct, and `appliesTo` going false for a reason *other* than delivery still loses the staged copy.
- **#1556** — a member owing a withheld delivery reads as `behind`, so `fleet-baseline` reports it as `did-not-converge` and the roster opens a drift issue with misleading remediation. {"number":1543,"title":"Enforce newest-first ordering in every pack's VERSIONS.md","body":"## Summary

A pack's `VERSIONS.md` is mostly newest-first, but nothing states or holds that, so rows get appended wherever the writing session happened to land and a long file's tail drifts out of sequence. `packs/claudinite-tasks/VERSIONS.md` had exactly that shape — descending from `60831.9` to `60824.1`, then four rows trailing out of order.

- Adds a new world-scope check, `pack-version-log-ordered` (`packs/claudinite-canon-curation/worldRules/pack-version-log-ordered.mjs`), which walks each pack's `VERSIONS.md` rows (reusing `rowVersions` from the existing `pack-version-bumped` rule) and flags any row that is newer than the row above it. Version comparison uses the repo's dotted-string `compareVersions`, never a float cast, so `'60820.10'` and `'60820.1'` compare correctly.
- Fixture test (`pack-version-log-ordered.test.mjs`) written first and run against the real tree, which failed on 9 packs before the sort (see the fixture's real-corpus test).
- Sorts every pack's `VERSIONS.md` rows newest-first: `basics`, `claudinite-canary-repo`, `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-lifecycle`, `claudinite-tasks`, `firebase`, `git-github`. Each diff is a pure reorder — verified the set of lines is identical before/after per file — so no row's text changes, no version number changes, and no `pack.mjs` version is bumped for any of these.
- `packs/claudinite-canon-curation/` (the pack this new check lives in, since #1541 just promoted it out of the canon's local packs) ships on its own version number, so its `pack.mjs` is bumped and it gets its own `VERSIONS.md` row and README checks-table entry.
- A new blocking rule needs either a migration record or a rehearsal fixture (`consumer-safe-changes.md` / the `consumer-safe-change` check) — this is genuinely additive, so the fixture is the honest answer. The existing `canon-home` rehearsal fixture (a member declaring `claudinite-canon-curation` over its own `packs/` shelf) now gives its shelf pack's `VERSIONS.md` a second, older row, so the fixture exercises a real newest-first comparison rather than a trivially-ordered single row.

Rebased onto `main` after #1541 landed mid-run; the check and its test moved from `.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/` to `packs/claudinite-canon-curation/` accordingly (git's rebase pointed this out directly), with the pack-relative import depth and `doc:` pointer adjusted to match its new siblings.

## Test plan

- [x] `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — 0 blocking findings (87 pre-existing advisories, unrelated)

{"number":1525,"title":"Mint host-page-interaction: driving a web page you don't own","body":"Part of growth-promote's run over ClaudiniteWebsite, CrosswordChat, EdFringeNow, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, LaughCounter, Shepherd (split from #1524 per the promote task's own convention: a new pack earns its own review surface).

CrosswordChat's local `host-page-adaptation` pack has grown a large, cohesive, genuinely uncovered body of practice: driving a web page you don't control — reading its DOM, driving it with synthetic input, watching it change, putting your own UI into its chrome. It doesn't fit any existing pack's territory:

- **chrome-extension** owns packaging/manifest/service-worker mechanics, not DOM interaction with an arbitrary host page.
- **headless-browser** owns driving a browser *you launched*, not a page you don't own running inside someone else's browser session.
- **html** owns hand-authored markup gotchas, not interaction.

The pack (`packs/host-page-interaction/`) generalizes it into 10 rules, stripped of the origin project's naming per the acid test in `generate-project-instructions` (no reader should be able to tell which project it came from): quarantining a host's DOM knowledge behind one module, casting a selector net rather than a single string, writing down verified-selector provenance, shipping a never-throwing health probe, mirroring the host in a fixture, verifying a write by re-reading it, building a full-fidelity synthetic keystroke, restoring toggled host state with a readable-state fallback, handling a host's own idle-timer/veil/splash lifecycle, and staying inert when off.

Declared by hand, no fingerprint (like `research-project`/`spec-driven-product`) — no single file signature reliably says "this code drives someone else's page."

`packs/directory.GENERATED.md` regenerated via `engine-tests/pack-directory.test.mjs`; `packs/README.md` carries the index row. `check_the_world.mjs` is clean (0 blocking).

{"number":1524,"title":"Promote 6 lessons from the fleet's local packs to canon","body":"growth-promote's central-stage run over the target members named in Context: ClaudiniteWebsite, CrosswordChat, EdFringeNow, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, LaughCounter, Shepherd.

Each item below is generalized from its origin repo's local pack, deduped against the whole corpus (most of these repos' local-pack content was already promoted in prior cycles — this is the residue), and routed to the pack whose territory it falls in.

**web-speech** (from CrosswordChat/`browser-speech`)
- OS-rendered TTS (`chrome.tts`) bypasses the browser's own echo cancellation entirely, since AEC only attenuates audio the browser itself rendered — needs an application-level echo guard (e.g. compare a heard transcript against what was just spoken).

**basics** (from LaughCounter/`laughcounter`, Shepherd/`shepherd`)
- Surface a shipped build's exact version+build identity from real build metadata, not a hand-maintained constant — two builds can share a version string.
- Before dropping a carried-over aggregate `GENERATED` file on "the next run recomputes it", check the recompute's own inputs cover the same historical span.

**node** (from GoogleCalendarEventCreator/`gcec`)
- A throwaway script needing a real project dependency can't live in an external scratchpad — Node's resolution walks up from the script's own location and never reaches the repo's `node_modules`.

**git-github** (from EdFringeNow/`edfringe`, Shepherd/`shepherd`, GoogleCalendarEventCreator/`gcec`)
- `gha/scheduled-failure-escalation` widens from `schedule:` alone to also catch `workflow_run:`/`repository_dispatch:` triggers — a workflow chained off another run or fired by an external dispatch is just as unwatched. Two new fixture cases prove it.
- `list_pull_requests`'s `merged` field is unreliable for landed-ness.
- `search_code` can undercount for an exhaustive enumeration task.
- Subscribe every PR a sweep leaves open, not a sample.
- A missing issue reference in the first commit is one `git commit --amend`, never a `git filter-branch`.
- Once a repo is confirmed to have no PR template, stop re-probing for one on every PR.

**claudinite-growth** (`unattended-agents` skill, from EdFringeNow/`edfringe`, Shepherd/`shepherd`)
- A dispatched subagent's "completed" notification can carry a placeholder final message rather than its real result.
- Check whether `AskUserQuestion`'s answer is already decided before firing it.

Every pack touched has its `version` bumped and a `VERSIONS.md` row. `node --test` on the touched packs' fixtures and `check_the_world.mjs` both pass clean (0 blocking).

**Notable rejections** (already covered elsewhere in the corpus, confirming strong prior promotion coverage): CrosswordChat's remaining `browser-speech`/`host-page-adaptation` rules (bar one new item mostly), EdFringeNow's GitHub-MCP-token-cap and CI-infra-outage findings, GoogleCalendarEventCreator's CDP/jsdom/generic-extractor findings, LaughCounter's `macos-audio`/`on-device-privacy` findings, and Shepherd's `git checkout  -- `, exact-title-search, and stale-main findings — all duplicate existing rules nearly verbatim.

**Deferred, not promoted this run**: CrosswordChat's `host-page-adaptation` pack is a large, cohesive, genuinely uncovered practice ("driving a host page you don't own") that doesn't fit any existing pack's territory — it needs a minted stub pack of its own, split into a separate PR per the promote task's own convention. Filed as a follow-up rather than rushed into this PR.

{"number":1513,"title":"Dissolve docs/skill-usage-metrics/DESIGN.md into the packs that own its subjects","body":"Closes #1169

## What changed

`docs/skill-usage-metrics/DESIGN.md` (769 lines) described a pipeline that is now built. Verifying section-by-section against the current tree (not #1169's evidence table, which was written against 2026-08-21's tree and predates the queue-rows migration and the usage-fold move into `claudinite-tasks`):

- **Almost everything was already covered**, in fresher and more complete form, by:

  - `packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/usage-fold/README.md` — the counting rules, the three-tier fold, "the check failures are the win", failure modes
  - `packs/claudinite-dashboard/README.md` — the reader half
  - Module headers on `engine/hooks/session-end-command.mjs`, `packs/claudinite-growth/session-end.mjs`, `packs/claudinite-tasks/run-record.mjs`, and the usage-fold task's own files

- **The one real gap**: nothing described how a canon-curation session should read the usage file for a skill-vs-prose or promotion judgment — `growth-promote/task.md` never mentions it. Added that paragraph to `claudinite-growth/README.md`'s existing "Skill-usage metrics" section.
- **Not carried anywhere new**: the old §3.5 (an ordering constraint for a one-time rollout gate that shipped and completed months ago — nothing forward-looking depends on it) and §10 (the owner-decision record) — verified every decision there is already implemented with its rationale stated in the current READMEs, so writing a second copy into the local pack's standing decisions would be pure duplication.

Swept all eight inbound `§`-numbered citations (grepped for `skill-usage-metrics`, confirmed zero hits after): six code-comment citations dropped (the surrounding comments already fully explain the behavior without the pointer), and two citations inside the frozen `docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md` historical record — dropped the citation only, left that record's own factual content untouched (it's an explicitly protected historical record per `.claudinite-settings.json`'s accept list).

Bumped both `claudinite-growth` and `claudinite-tasks` pack versions with `VERSIONS.md` rows, since both are edited.

## Worth deciding separately

Per the issue's own note: the same argument applies to the other five `docs/*/DESIGN.md` files (`tasks-dispatch` alone is 1,958 lines). This PR does **not** sweep them — that's a much larger call the issue explicitly asked to leave to the owner.

{"number":1556,"title":"A member owing a withheld delivery reads as "behind", so a fleet baseline reports it as failed","body":"Follow-up to #1545. That fix stops a pack being stamped while it still owes a withheld workflow file, so the record stays in range and the delivery is re-staged rather than lost. The consequence is a member that has converged correctly but deliberately reports an older pack version for a cycle — and sheepdog has no way to tell that apart from a member that is failing to converge.

## What misreads it

`packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs`, `classifyFreshness`, compares each installed pack version against canon and returns `behind` on any gap. A member holding `claudinite-tasks` while canon has moved can never read `FRESH`.

Two things follow:

1. **`fleet-baseline` reports the member as failed.** `follow-to-current.mjs` polls freshness until every dispatched member reaches canon's versions, then reports `did-not-converge` for those that did not. A member that withheld a file will not reach them until the *next* cycle, after the apply stage delivers — so a forced baseline reports it as a failure. That is precisely the lever used to push a withheld delivery out, reporting the target members as broken.

2. **The roster opens a drift issue with misleading remediation.** The `behind` fix text tells the reader the self-refresh is not landing and to check the repo's recent scheduler runs. The self-refresh *is* landing; a delivery is pending on another credential. It self-closes once the stamp catches up, having sent someone to look at the wrong thing.

## Why "behind" is not simply wrong

The member genuinely has not received the version — that is the honest reading, and #1545 exists because the opposite reading (stamped, therefore delivered) is what made a broken fleet look healthy. This is not a request to report such a member as fresh.

What is missing is a **third state**. "Converged, delivery pending" is neither `fresh` nor `behind`, and collapsing it into `behind` loses the distinction that decides whether anyone should act.

## Shape of the fix

Make the hold visible so it can be classified rather than inferred: have the member record that a delivery is owed (and for which pack), and give `classifyFreshness` an `owes-delivery` state with its own remediation text. `follow-to-current` then treats it as a terminal, non-failing outcome — the baseline's job is done once the deterministic half has landed and the apply stage is raised.

Worth deciding at the same time: whether a member that has owed a delivery for several cycles should escalate, since that is a real stall and currently indistinguishable from one healthy pending cycle.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1556","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["bug"],"assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-09-01T10:26:57Z","updated_at":"2026-09-01T10:26:57Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1555,"title":"The staging sweep deletes on "I didn't write it this pass", which is not the same as "it was delivered"","body":"Follow-up to #1545, which fixed the version-stamp half of that incident. The sweep's own criterion is still wrong, and it can reproduce the same silent loss from a different trigger.

## The criterion

`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/pack-update.mjs` sweeps the staging directory of anything this run did not stage:

```js
const stagedNow = new Set(withheld.map(stagedAt));
for (const stale of stagedFiles(targetRoot)) {
  if (stagedNow.has(stale)) continue;
  rmSync(join(targetRoot, stale), { force: true });
}
```

Its comment states the premise: *"a file staged by an earlier cycle was either delivered or abandoned, and either way the record that staged it would stage it again."*

That conflates two opposite facts. "This run did not stage it" is true both when the file **was delivered** (good — sweep it) and when the record **stopped matching for some other reason** (bad — this is the only copy of computed content).

## Where it still loses content

`appliesTo` on the vars-bag records tests `text.includes(HOLD) && !text.includes('CLAUDINITE_VARS:')`. It goes false for reasons other than a successful delivery:

- the anchor line drifts — the operator hold is renamed, or the wiring converge regenerates the region
- someone adds a `CLAUDINITE_VARS:` comment, or a partial edit
- the executor is momentarily unreadable or renamed, so `applyRewrites` hits `if (text == null) continue`

In each case the record does not re-stage, the sweep deletes the staged file, and — because nothing was withheld — the pack is stamped, putting the record out of range. That is byte-for-byte the #1545 outcome with a different trigger.

#1545's stamp hold narrows the window but does not make the criterion correct; the protection (`stagedNow`) is conditional on precisely the premise that failed.

## The fix

Delete a staged file only when the destination demonstrably carries its content, rather than when this pass happened not to write it. A file whose destination still lacks it is an outstanding delivery, not a leftover.

This needs care with one existing behaviour: `engine-tests/pack-update.test.mjs`'s *"the retired staging directory is swept, whatever an earlier cycle left in it"* covers a genuine leftover from the retired lane whose destination will never match. That case wants an explicit rule (out of range for the right reason), not the current catch-all.

Also worth scoping: the sweep is unconditional across flows, with nothing limiting it to files the pack flow owns.

## Second, smaller gap

An **engine**-flow record gets no hold at all. `flowOf` returns `{ flow: 'engine' }` with no `pack`, and the guard added in #1545 is `if (owedBy)`. Today the engine flow cannot withhold — `engine-update.mjs` passes `env: {}`, so workflow writes are skipped — while it stamps unconditionally. If the engine flow ever gains the withhold lane, it inherits the original bug.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1555","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["bug"],"assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-09-01T10:26:40Z","updated_at":"2026-09-01T10:26:40Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1496,"title":"Verify in production: the executor's `toJSON(vars)` line does not get the workflow held for approval","body":"Original-issue: #1492
In-production-when: `missingbulb/Claudinite` has at least one `Claudinite executor` workflow run whose head sha is `e846728` or later (the squash of #1494, which put `CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}` into `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`).
Verify: List those executor runs. PASS = every one of them created at least one job and none concluded `action_required`. FAIL = any run concluded `action_required`, or concluded in about a second having created zero jobs — that is GitHub's malicious-workflow hold, and it means `toJSON(vars)` is flagged the way `toJSON(secrets)` was in #1336.
Not-before: 2026-09-01T06:15:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day
Model: sonnet

## Why this could not be watched now

#1494 added one static line to the executor's work step:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}
```

The reader is fully unit-tested against synthetic JSON, so nothing about *parsing* a bag needs production. What no test can reach is the claim the whole change rests on: **that serialising the `vars` context does not trip GitHub's [malicious-workflow detection](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-github-actions-holds-potentially-malicious-workflows-for-approval/)** the way serialising `secrets` did in #1336.

That claim is inference plus field evidence, not a guarantee:

- GitHub publishes no detection signals, thresholds or false-positive rate.
- `vars` is the context GitHub's own docs define as non-sensitive and render unmasked in build logs, so the exfiltration reading does not apply — but that is our reasoning, not GitHub's statement.
- `packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml` and `static-site-deploy-pages.yml` have both passed `toJSON(vars)` since before the safeguard shipped without a park — strong evidence, from a different workflow than this one.

The failure mode is why this is worth a run rather than a shrug: a held run creates **zero jobs** and concludes `action_required` in about a second, which from the queue's side is indistinguishable from "nothing was pickable". #1336 ate executor runs in two repos for hours before anyone noticed, and #1330 mis-diagnosed it as a repository setting. Nothing red appears. Only reading run conclusions finds it.

The canon's scheduler is on `44 5,17 * * *`, so its drain dispatches the executor twice a day; `Not-before:` is aimed just past the first tick after the merge.

## Instructions to the run

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the Actions API — the real run list, never a merge, a green CI job or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`.
   - Passes: comment the run ids and conclusions you actually read, and close this issue as completed.
   - Fails: reopen #1492 with a comment naming the held run, its conclusion and its job count, and say that `toJSON(vars)` must come out of `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml` and `packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/claudinite-executor.yml` — the fleet is exposed to a silent park until it does. Comment here linking that, then close this issue as completed.
3. **Not yet live** (no executor run at or past that sha) → set `Not-before:` to the instant you are reading this at plus `Retry-every:`, clear this issue's `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. No comment.

You are mining captured agent↔user conversation logs for durable lessons, as the "conversation half" of a Claudinite growth-extract run on repo missingbulb/Claudinite. RESEARCH ONLY — do not write/edit any files, do not post any comments. You're in a git checkout at /home/user/Claudinite with the `origin/conversation-logs` branch already fetched locally.

## Reading the logs
Each file below is a JSONL capture of part of a session's transcript (tool calls, tool results, assistant/user messages, with per-entry timestamps and token usage). Read each with:
```
git show origin/conversation-logs:<filename>
```
(Note: this could be a big file — if `git show` output is huge, pipe to a file in /tmp and use grep/python to search it rather than loading it all into your own context at once — e.g. `git show origin/conversation-logs:<filename> > /tmp/cap.jsonl` then `python3 -c "import json; ..."` or `jq` to pull out just message text/roles/timestamps.)

Files to read (all from roughly 2026-08-31T09:45Z to 2026-08-31T11:32Z UTC — this is the "last 24h" window of a daily extraction run):

2026-08-31T1132Z--issue-1501--05913db3-8428-5927-bc61-c9896f37cd3d.jsonl

The `issue-<n>` in the filename is the GitHub issue this session's work is tracked under (you'll need this number to report provenance — where a landed lesson's summary would be posted).

## What to look for — friction signals
Read each session's turns AND actions (not just what got built, but how the loop went) and hunt for:

1. **Misunderstandings**: a clarifying-question round-trip, the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"), the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it, an AskUserQuestion whose answer was obviously the default.
2. **Suboptimal agent actions**: the agent backtracked, did redundant/repeated work, re-ran a command that had already failed for a knowable reason, reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit, reinvented something the codebase already provided, missed an existing convention and got corrected.
3. **Long wall-time waits** (measure with real timestamps from the log, don't estimate): independent ops run serially with no dependency, a padded fixed sleep, a process waited out after its result was already in hand, blind long polling, re-running an already-green check.

Each signal converts to a **durable fix** — a rule, convention, default, or pointer — only if it would make the NEXT similar session faster/clearer without the same round-trip. A one-off annoyance specific to that session's exact circumstances doesn't qualify. Most sessions will yield nothing — that's normal.

## Output format
For each candidate lesson:
1. **Source**: issue number + session id (for provenance — where the summary comment would post)
2. **Evidence**: what happened, with any measured wall-time numbers if it's an efficiency finding
3. **Proposed rule**: one terse imperative sentence (trigger → directive) as if going into RULES.md
4. **200-word-max provenance summary**: what was asked, what went wrong/got corrected, why the rule follows — this is what would get posted on the issue if the lesson lands
5. **Confidence**: how sure this is genuinely novel vs. already-known

If a session yields nothing, just note it briefly (one line) — don't force lessons. Keep the final report as a tight bullet list of real candidates, not a narrative of every session.

RESEARCH ONLY — do not write/edit any files, do not post any comments. You're in a git checkout at /home/user/Claudinite with the `origin/conversation-logs` branch already fetched locally.

## Reading the logs
Each file below is a JSONL capture of part of a session's transcript (tool calls, tool results, assistant/user messages, with per-entry timestamps and token usage). Read each with:
```

```
(Note: this could be a big file — if `git show` output is huge, pipe to a file in /tmp and use grep/python to search it rather than loading it all into your own context at once — e.g. `git show origin/conversation-logs:<filename> > /tmp/cap.jsonl` then `python3 -c "import json; ..."` or `jq` to pull out just message text/roles/timestamps.)

Files to read (all from roughly 2026-08-31T09:45Z to 2026-08-31T11:32Z UTC — this is the "last 24h" window of a daily extraction run):

The `issue-<n>` in the filename is the GitHub issue this session's work is tracked under (you'll need this number to report provenance — where a landed lesson's summary would be posted).

## What to look for — friction signals
Read each session's turns AND actions (not just what got built, but how the loop went) and hunt for:

1. **Misunderstandings**: a clarifying-question round-trip, the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"), the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it, an AskUserQuestion whose answer was obviously the default.
2. **Suboptimal agent actions**: the agent backtracked, did redundant/repeated work, re-ran a command that had already failed for a knowable reason, reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit, reinvented something the codebase already provided, missed an existing convention and got corrected.
3. **Long wall-time waits** (measure with real timestamps from the log, don't estimate): independent ops run serially with no dependency, a padded fixed sleep, a process waited out after its result was already in hand, blind long polling, re-running an already-green check.

Each signal converts to a **durable fix** — a rule, convention, default, or pointer — only if it would make the NEXT similar session faster/clearer without the same round-trip. A one-off annoyance specific to that session's exact circumstances doesn't qualify. Most sessions will yield nothing — that's normal.

## Output format
For each candidate lesson:
1. **Source**: issue number + session id (for provenance — where the summary comment would post)
2. **Evidence**: what happened, with any measured wall-time numbers if it's an efficiency finding
3. **Proposed rule**: one terse imperative sentence (trigger → directive) as if going into RULES.md
4. **200-word-max provenance summary**: what was asked, what went wrong/got corrected, why the rule follows — this is what would get posted on the issue if the lesson lands
5. **Confidence**: how sure this is genuinely novel vs. already-known

If a session yields nothing, just note it briefly (one line) — don't force lessons. Keep the final report as a tight bullet list of real candidates, not a narrative of every session.

- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.

Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. - repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.

Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. - artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. # Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
59	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. This is the first rung to try for any
60	   lesson whose whole logic is "these patterns over these files", and most captured conditions are. Give it
61	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
62	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
63	   else's next change, not this run's.
64	2. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
65	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
66	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
67	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
68	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
69	3. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
70	4. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
71	
72	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
73	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
74	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
75	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
76	
77	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
78	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
79	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
80	
81	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
82	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small.** Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every
83	session in every repo that declares the pack, forever, whether or not it ever applies — so a pass adds *at
84	most two*, each one sentence: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence clause only where the rule can't
85	be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph to land has not been understood well enough to be
86	a rule yet; the evidence behind it belongs in the PR body and the issue, never in the rule.
87	If more than two candidates clear every bar above, write the two strongest and drop the rest — they will
88	recur if they were real.
89	
90	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
91	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
92	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
93	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
94	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
95	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
96	
97	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
98	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
99	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
100	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
101	tidy-repo pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
102	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
103	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
104	
105	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
106	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
107	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
108	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
109	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
110	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
111	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
112	
113	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
114	
115	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
116	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
117	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
118	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
119

content.text:
Not present verbatim — closest existing entries are about *removing/renaming* an export (shim it) and *adding a spec-key* (write the declaration to work without it), but neither covers a pack *importing* a brand-new engine export by name. That's a distinct failure mode.

## Report

Read PRs #1549, #1544, #1541, #1529, #1523, #1534 (diff + comments + reviews — all had empty review/comment threads, so no reviewer-correction signal in any of them) and issues #1556, #1495, #1555, #1496 (all automation-authored `verify-in-production` issues or fresh bug reports, no human back-and-forth).

Candidates:

- **Source**: #1544 (introduced bug) → #1549 (fixed it), same day, both merged.
- **Evidence**: #1544 split `unplacedSpecKeys` out of `pattern-rules.mjs` and had the new `declared-check-spec-keys` world rule consume it via a **named** import (`import { unplacedSpecKeys } from '...pattern-rules.mjs'`). #1549's body: "a named import of an absent export is a **link-time `SyntaxError`**... which fails the `pack-manifests` probe, which parks the converge" — because the pack lane (nightly) and engine lane (release-only) ship on separate cadences, so a member can hold the new pack code against an engine that predates the export. Fix: switch to `import * as patternRules` plus a `typeof engine.unplacedSpecKeys === 'function'` capability guard.
- **Proposed rule**: **Adding a pack module that consumes a brand-new engine helper export** — import the engine module as a namespace and guard the call with a capability check (`typeof ns.fn === 'function'`), never a named import; the pack and engine lanes deliver on separate cycles, so a named import of an export that hasn't shipped yet is a link-time `SyntaxError` that faults the whole pack and parks the converge.
- **Confidence**: Medium-high. Not a restated existing rule — the corpus already covers *removing/renaming* an engine export (leave a shim) and *adding a spec-key* (write declarations to tolerate absence), but not this inverse case of a pack immediately depending on a fresh engine export. Novel enough to be worth landing, though narrow to this cross-lane-delivery architecture (may only matter to Claudinite itself, not portable).

- **Source**: #1555 (open issue, follow-up to #1545/#1482 incident).
- **Evidence**: `pack-update.mjs`'s staging sweep deletes any staged file this run didn't re-stage, on the premise "either delivered or abandoned, and either way the record that staged it would stage it again." Issue shows that premise is false: the match condition (`appliesTo`) can go false for reasons unrelated to delivery (anchor text drifts, a file becomes unreadable, someone edits the target) — silently losing the only copy of computed content, "byte-for-byte the #1545 outcome with a different trigger."
- **Proposed rule**: **Writing a sweep that deletes a staged/pending artifact because this pass didn't rewrite it** — delete only when the destination demonstrably now carries that content; treat "not restaged" and "delivered" as different facts, since a match condition can stop matching for reasons other than success.
- **Confidence**: Medium. Genuinely durable and generalizable (a sweep/cleanup correctness pattern), but sourced from an *unresolved* issue body rather than a landed fix or reviewer correction — flag for the judging agent to confirm it's not already implicit in existing "Deleting a writer" / idempotent-pipeline rules before landing.

Everything else yielded nothing durable:
- **#1529 / #1523** (the version-collision incident, #1482) — both already fully resolved by new blocking checks (`pack-version-claimed-once`, world scope; `ci-work-scope.mjs` judging pushes against pre-push base) that now pin the exact shape. Per the stated bar, an already-enforced check is not a lesson.
- **#1541** — large mechanical promotion of a local pack to canon-shelf-generic; no review discussion, no wrong turn.
- **#1534** — new coded-verification feature, no review discussion, nothing corrected.
- **#1556, #1495, #1496** — automation-authored issues/comments only (queue bot, executor bot), no human discussion. #1556 is a real but narrow/project-specific classification gap (fleet freshness state machine), not generalizable.

input.prompt:
You are mining captured agent↔user conversation logs for durable lessons, as the "conversation half" of a Claudinite growth-extract run on repo missingbulb/Claudinite. RESEARCH ONLY — do not write/edit any files, do not post any comments. You're in a git checkout at /home/user/Claudinite with the `origin/conversation-logs` branch already fetched locally.

## Reading the logs
Each file below is a JSONL capture of part of a session's transcript (tool calls, tool results, assistant/user messages, with per-entry timestamps and token usage). Read each with:
```

- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. - repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.

Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. - artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
