Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

content.text: First research agent back with candidates. Waiting on the remaining five before I start curating.

## Summary of research

All 6 PRs are single-author, agent-authored, and merged with **zero review comments and zero formal reviews** (`get_comments`/`get_reviews` returned `[]` for all six). Everything of substance lives in the PR bodies themselves (rich self-documentation) — there was no "reviewer corrected author" dynamic to mine. The 6 touched issues likewise carry only bot-machinery comments (queue/claim/handoff), except #1542, which has one owner comment restating an already-known "stacked-PR/mid-run structural drift" class already covered by corpus (`pack-version-bumped` lesson). #1550, #1547, #1545, #1458, #1517 have no human discussion at all.

## Candidate lessons

- **Source**: PR #1516 (`fd5e737`), closes #1515
  **Evidence**: "Two janitor rules stamped `task:status:needs-human-decision` for situations no human decided... Both now park `task:status:needs-human-failure`, and the janitor no longer writes a `decision` park at all... Rule E can drain these [failure parks]. A later clean run of the task is proof the earlier one is no longer broken. Under `decision` that proof was inadmissible and the parks accumulated." 93 open `decision` parks fleet-wide traced to this bug.
  **Proposed rule**: **Choosing a park/status kind for an automated observation** — never stamp a kind reserved for genuine human debt (e.g. `decision`) for something a machine merely noticed (a timeout, a torn transition); a human-debt kind can never be superseded by a later clean run, so a misclassified machine-observed park accumulates forever instead of self-clearing.
  **Confidence**: Medium-high — this is a specific, non-obvious failure mode (silent unbounded accumulation from a classification error) not obviously already stated in the corpus, though it's adjacent to the existing "finer-grained classification of a catch-all state" rule.

- **Source**: PR #1540, closes #1539, refs #1511/#1494
  **Evidence**: A regression test asserted the *literal retired sentence* (`assert.match(task, /never move a file into .github.workflows./i, ...)`) as proof the workflow-delivery lane stayed retired. "The suite stayed green through #1511 because it required the contradiction to be present." Result: three artifacts disagreed, the fleet split 8/5 on the same brief, both halves reasoning correctly from different halves of it.
  **Proposed rule**: **Writing a regression test that pins a policy decision** — assert the *behavior/invariant* the decision requires, never a literal quoted sentence copied from one doc; a sentence-matching test stays green forever even while a sibling doc states the opposite, so it certifies a split-brain contradiction instead of catching one.
  **Confidence**: Medium — genuinely novel angle on test design, though it overlaps with the existing "purge every place that states the old decision" rule (which covers the sweep, not the test-authoring failure mode that let the sweep get skipped).

- **Source**: PR #1465, closes #942
  **Evidence**: "The cache key was the trap. That workflow skips the build when a hash over the mount and settings is unchanged, and no file hash covers a repository variable. Without folding them into the key, changing either would hit the cache, skip the build, and leave the site serving the previous client id with nothing to show for it."
  **Proposed rule**: **Keying a build/deploy cache off a content hash** — fold in every non-file input the build actually reads (repo/env variables, secrets-derived config), not just tracked files; a hash that only covers the mount silently serves stale output whenever a variable changes.
  **Confidence**: High — small, easy-to-miss, and generically reusable beyond this repo.

- **Source**: PR #1465
  **Evidence**: "enables the `workers.dev` route (previews off — a preview URL is a second origin able to mint tokens)."
  **Proposed rule**: **Deploying an endpoint that mints or exchanges auth tokens** — disable preview/staging deployments on the platform (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, etc.); a preview URL is a live second origin outside the allowlist that can mint real tokens.
  **Confidence**: Medium — solid security point, narrower applicability (only relevant to token-minting endpoints on platforms with auto preview URLs).

- **Source**: PR #1522, closes #1518
  **Evidence**: "The anchor is the operator hold, not that marker. Anchoring to the marker would put the bag inside the region the wiring converge regenerates, where the next converge would overwrite it... Idempotency lives in `appliesTo`... the version gate alone is not enough."
  **Proposed rule**: **Inserting a one-time block into a file another process regenerates a marked region of** — anchor outside that regenerated region (so the next regen doesn't erase the insert), and gate re-application on literal content-presence, not a version check alone, since split/join insertion is not naturally idempotent.
  **Confidence**: Low-medium — useful pattern but narrowly tied to this migration-record mechanism and already pinned by the PR's own tests (borderline "already-settled" per the stated bar).

Everything else (PR #1528, #1532, and issues #1517/#1550/#1547/#1545/#1542/#1458) yielded nothing durable beyond what's already codified in the corpus or already settled by the change's own tests/skill — no forced report there.

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
59	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. This is the first rung to try for any
60	   lesson whose whole logic is "these patterns over these files", and most captured conditions are. Give it
61	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
62	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
63	   else's next change, not this run's.
64	2. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
65	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
66	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
67	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
68	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
69	3. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
70	4. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
71	
72	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
73	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
74	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
75	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
76	
77	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
78	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
79	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
80	
81	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
82	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small.** Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every
83	session in every repo that declares the pack, forever, whether or not it ever applies — so a pass adds *at
84	most two*, each one sentence: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence clause only where the rule can't
85	be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph to land has not been understood well enough to be
86	a rule yet; the evidence behind it belongs in the PR body and the issue, never in the rule.
87	If more than two candidates clear every bar above, write the two strongest and drop the rest — they will
88	recur if they were real.
89	
90	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
91	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
92	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
93	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
94	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
95	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
96	
97	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
98	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
99	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
100	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
101	tidy-repo pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
102	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
103	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
104	
105	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
106	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
107	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
108	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
109	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
110	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
111	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
112	
113	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
114	
115	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
116	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
117	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
118	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
59	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. This is the first rung to try for any
60	   lesson whose whole logic is "these patterns over these files", and most captured conditions are. Give it
61	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
62	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
63	   else's next change, not this run's.
64	2. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
65	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
66	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
67	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
68	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
69	3. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
70	4. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
71	
72	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
73	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
74	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
75	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
76	
77	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
78	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
79	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
80	
81	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
82	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small.** Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every
83	session in every repo that declares the pack, forever, whether or not it ever applies — so a pass adds *at
84	most two*, each one sentence: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence clause only where the rule can't
85	be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph to land has not been understood well enough to be
86	a rule yet; the evidence behind it belongs in the PR body and the issue, never in the rule.
87	If more than two candidates clear every bar above, write the two strongest and drop the rest — they will
88	recur if they were real.
89	
90	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
91	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
92	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
93	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
94	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
95	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
96	
97	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
98	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
99	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
100	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
101	tidy-repo pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
102	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
103	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
104	
105	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
106	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
107	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
108	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
109	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
110	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
111	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
112	
113	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
114	
115	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
116	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
117	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
118	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
119

## Findings

Both merged-PR batches (#1521, #1502, #1511, #1503, #1494, #1493) have **zero review comments and zero reviews** — every one is a solo-author, solo-merge PR whose "lesson" is already written into `RULES.md`/`VERSIONS.md` as part of the same diff. Per the task's own bar ("an already-settled, already-enforced choice is NOT a lesson"), none of these six yields anything to extract — the corpus already states exactly what they'd teach (e.g. #1521 → the `Wanting to verify or read something across members` rule already in `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`; #1503 → `Converging a work item from a session`, also already there).

Touched issues (Part 3) are almost all queue-bot transition logs or single owner comments; the substantive ones (#1236, #1469, #1353) are all instances of the *same* cross-repo-scope-denial failure that PR #1521 already fixed and documented — no new signal. #1264/#1295/#1333 are plain "needs owner decision, no artifact resolves it" parks — already-known pattern, nothing durable to add.

The one genuinely new, non-trivial finding is in **PR #1546** (open, unmerged, tracks issue #1545) — and unlike the six merged PRs, this one has **not** yet written its lesson into `RULES.md`, so it's a real candidate.

## Candidate lessons

- **Source**: PR #1546 / issue #1545 (open, not yet merged)
- **Evidence**: A migration record staged a workflow-file write for later delivery by a different credential (the apply stage), but the converge run stamped the owning pack's version *immediately* regardless. Because `migrationApplies` is `want > have`, that stamp permanently took the record out of range the instant it landed — and the *next* cycle's staging-sweep then deleted the staged file as a stale leftover, since nothing else referenced it. Every signal stayed green throughout; five members silently lost the delivered content with no way back short of hand-authoring a brand-new migration record above their stamped version.
- **Proposed rule**: **Staging part of a change for delivery by a separate, later mechanism (a different credential, a different run)** — never mark/stamp/version-advance the owning unit as delivered until that deferred part actually lands, because a premature stamp against a `want > have` gate takes the record out of range forever, and a generic "clean up what I didn't just write" sweep then deletes the only remaining copy of the undelivered content — silently, with every check green.
- **Confidence**: High novelty/durability. This is a general two-phase-commit-style footgun (stamp-before-confirm + generic sweep-of-orphans), not specific to Claudinite's migration engine, and it is not yet recorded anywhere in the corpus I read (RULES.md is untouched by this PR).

- **Source**: same PR #1546 / issue #1545, second fix in the same branch
- **Evidence**: The update worker's "nothing changed, skip the PR" short-circuit tested only `git status --porcelain` on the working tree. A re-staging cycle can leave the tree byte-identical to a still-open branch (the staged bytes are already committed there) while a delivery is still owed — and the code that raises the "please deliver this" request runs *after* that early-return, so the guard would have silently swallowed the very request meant to close the loop, reintroducing the same silent loss one step further along.
- **Proposed rule**: **Writing an early-exit "nothing to do" guard keyed on a diff or dirty-tree check** — verify every terminal/outcome branch actually flows through that guard correctly, in particular one whose real effect lives outside the diffed tree (a written request, an API call, an issue update); a diff-based guard sees only file content and will swallow an outcome whose work is done by a side channel.
- **Confidence**: Medium — durable and reusable as a general "early-return guards must cover every terminal path" principle, but narrower/more implementation-adjacent than the first finding; likely worth folding into the first as a consequence rather than a fully separate rule.

Everything else surveyed (Part 1 in full, Part 2's #1543/#1525/#1524/#1513, and Part 3's remaining issues) yielded nothing durable beyond what the repo's own local-pack `RULES.md` already states.

def parse_ts(ts):
    if not ts: return None
    try:
        return datetime.fromisoformat(ts.replace('Z','+00:00'))

        return None

def trunc(s, n=300):
    if s is None: return ""

import json, sys

def trunc(s, n=200):
    if s is None: return ""
    s = str(s)
    return s if len(s) <= n else s[:n] + "...[%d chars]" % len(s)

def main(path, textlen=300):
    with open(path) as f:
        for i, line in enumerate(f):
            line = line.strip()
            if not line: continue
            try:
                e = json.loads(line)
            except Exception as ex:
                print(f"[{i}] PARSE ERROR {ex}")
                continue
            ts = e.get('timestamp') or e.get('ts') or e.get('time')
            typ = e.get('type') or e.get('role')
            out = f"[{i}] ts={ts} type={typ}"
            # try common shapes
            msg = e.get('message')
            if isinstance(msg, dict):
                role = msg.get('role')
                content = msg.get('content')
                if isinstance(content, str):
                    out += f" role={role} text={trunc(content, textlen)!r}"
                elif isinstance(content, list):
                    for c in content:
                        if not isinstance(c, dict): continue
                        ctype = c.get('type')
                        if ctype == 'text':
                            out += f"\n    TEXT[{role}]: {trunc(c.get('text'), textlen)!r}"
                        elif ctype == 'tool_use':
                            out += f"\n    TOOL_USE: {c.get('name')} input={trunc(json.dumps(c.get('input', {})), textlen)}"
                        elif ctype == 'tool_result':
                            cc = c.get('content')
                            if isinstance(cc, list):
                                cc = ' '.join(trunc(x.get('text',''),100) for x in cc if isinstance(x,dict))
                            out += f"\n    TOOL_RESULT: {trunc(cc, textlen)}"
                        else:
                            out += f"\n    OTHER[{ctype}]: {trunc(c, 100)}"
            else:
                # fallback: dump top-level keys briefly
                keys = list(e.keys())
                out += f" keys={keys}"
                if 'text' in e:
                    out += f" text={trunc(e['text'], textlen)!r}"
            print(out)

## Summary

Read all six captures (issues 349, 359, 364, 366, 368, 373 — 2026‑07‑19/20 window). Five of six sessions surfaced friction that maps onto rules **already present** in the current `claudinite/RULES.md` — in fact, two of the sessions (issue #349, PR #348 "Pack independence…"; issue #364, PR #361 "canon-curation move…") read like the very origin incidents for several standing rules already quoted verbatim in this repo's current CLAUDE.md context (the pack-independence-via-barriers rule, the "owner reversing a standing decision" rule, and the "canon pack naming a home-only local pack" rule). No action needed there — flagging as corroboration that those rules are earning their keep, not as new findings.

One genuinely new, repeated pattern surfaced across three separate sessions in the same 24h window:

### Candidate: stale `origin/main` causes a false `squash-merge-history` blocking finding

- **Source**: recurs in issue #366 (session `1952b8c3…`), issue #368 (session `e618ea16…`), and issue #373 (session `9c126afc…`) — three distinct sessions, same day.
- **Evidence** (with measured wall-time):
  - Issue #366: `node checks/run.mjs` run at 20:41:09 flags `squash-merge-history` on a pre-existing merge commit (`8ba0881`, from PR #339, already on `main`). Agent inspects `git log`, concludes it's stale, fetches, re-runs clean at 20:41:52 (~43s lost).
  - Issue #368: same finding at 21:32:11; agent reasons it's "pre-existing" *without* fetching, pushes anyway — then the Stop hook re-fires the **identical** finding at 21:33:04, forcing a second detour (fetch → re-verify → amend → force-push) ending 21:33:57 (~1m47s lost across two passes).
  - Issue #373: same finding investigated 10:11:23–10:12:24 (~1 min lost).
  - Root cause each time: the local `origin/main` tracking ref is stale (this repo lands merges every few minutes from many concurrent sessions), so the `squash-merge-history` check's diff range reaches back across an already-landed merge and misreports it as newly introduced by the branch.
- **Proposed rule**: Before running `node checks/run.mjs`/trusting a `squash-merge-history` finding, `git fetch origin main` first — this repo's `main` advances fast enough that a stale local ref routinely misflags an already-landed merge commit as newly introduced by the branch.
- **200-word provenance summary**: Across three independent sessions on 2026‑07‑19/20 (issues #366, #368, #373), `node checks/run.mjs` reported a `[BLOCKING] squash-merge-history` finding pointing at merge commit `8ba0881` (from long-landed PR #339). In every case the actual cause was the same: the session's local `origin/main` tracking ref was stale — this repo lands merges every few minutes from many concurrent Claude Code sessions — so the check's `origin/main..HEAD` diff range reached back across a merge that was already on `main`, misreading it as introduced by the current branch. Each session spent a full diagnostic detour (inspecting `git log`, reasoning about whether the merge was "mine," then `git fetch origin main` to confirm and clear it) before re-running checks clean. In issue #368 the agent skipped the fetch after its first diagnosis and paid for it twice — the Stop hook re-fired the identical finding a few minutes later. The fix is procedural: fetch `origin/main` before trusting this specific check's verdict, rather than diagnosing staleness after the fact each time.
- **Confidence**: High that this is genuinely novel (no existing rule addresses fetching-before-checks specifically) and high that it's a real recurring pattern (3 independent occurrences, one session even repeated it internally). Worth considering as a `checks/run.mjs`-side fix (auto-fetch, or a friendlier failure message) rather than pure prose, since prose compliance was already imperfect within the same session it was diagnosed in (issue #368).

All other sessions (issue #349, #359, #364) yielded no new candidates — their friction (structured-decision corrections, comment-classification/task-lifecycle omissions caught by the Stop hook) already matches mechanisms or prose currently in the corpus.
